messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amir is a 54-year-old community organizer, married, and a father of three grown children, who came to therapy at the urging of his wife after months of escalating tension at home. For the past year, he has been living with a kind of dread that he cannot shake, a sense that the ground beneath him is unstable. He is a tall, broad-shouldered man who speaks with a careful, measured tone, but his hands tremble slightly as he describes what happened two years ago.

The event itself was a betrayal so complete that Amir still struggles to hold it in his mind as a single story. He had been in a romantic relationship with a man named Khalid, a fellow activist he had known for years and trusted implicitly. One evening, after a community meeting, they drove to a secluded spot near the river to talk. What began as an argument over a political disagreement turned quickly into something Amir had never imagined possible. Khalid, a man Amir had loved and confided in, struck him repeatedly in the face and ribs, then pinned him down and choked him until Amir saw stars. The assault lasted perhaps ten minutes, but in Amir’s memory, it exists only in fragments: the sound of his own ribs cracking, the feel of gravel digging into his back, the sight of Khalid’s face twisted into a mask of rage, and then—nothing. He remembers coming to on the ground, alone in the dark, with the distant sound of a helicopter overhead, its rotors thumping in the silence.

Amir never reported the assault. He was too ashamed, too certain that people would blame him for being naive. In the weeks that followed, he found himself unable to go near the riverbank where it happened. He started taking long detours on his commute, adding twenty minutes to his drive, because even the street that led in that direction made his chest tighten. At home, he began closing the blinds at dusk. He had never been afraid of the dark before, but now he could not bear a room without light. He told himself it was just a phase, that he was being sensible. But the memories kept coming without warning. He would be standing at the kitchen sink, washing dishes, and suddenly he would hear Khalid’s voice in his head—not words, just the sound of his breathing, heavy and fast. Or he would be driving and the thrum of a helicopter overhead would send a jolt through him so sharp that he would have to pull over.

Amir began to change the way he dressed. He had always been a man who took pride in his appearance, but now he bought loose, dark jackets and hooded sweatshirts, even in summer. He wore them zipped up, the hood often half-up, because he had come to believe that if people could not see him clearly, they would not notice him, and if they did not notice him, they could not hurt him. His wife noticed, of course. She asked him why he was dressing like he was hiding, and he told her he was just cold. She did not press, but she saw the way he scanned every room they entered, his eyes moving from face to face, cataloging threats. At community meetings—the very work that had once given him purpose—Amir now sat with his back to the wall, watching the door. He had started to believe that what happened to him was not an accident of circumstance but a revelation of something fundamental about himself. He was the kind of person people could betray. He was the kind of person who deserved to be hurt. His old belief that the world was basically fair, that people were basically good, had been shattered, and he could not find the pieces.

The consequences have been severe. Six months ago, Amir stepped down from leading a major coalition campaign because he could no longer tolerate the unpredictability of public spaces. His colleagues were confused; they thought he had burned out. He did not correct them. At home, he has become irritable and withdrawn. His wife has told him, gently, that she feels like she is living with a stranger. What finally brought Amir to therapy was a moment last week when his youngest daughter, visiting for dinner, reached out to touch his arm and he flinched so violently that he knocked over his glass. He saw the hurt in her face, and he knew he could not keep pretending that everything was fine. He is terrified that the person he used to be is gone forever, but he is even more afraid of what he might become if he does not find a way to put the pieces back together.
